## Introduction

Many elderly adults experience a decline in function as they age. Over the past decades, researchers have sought to address factors that may influence this. In this analysis we reference a study that focuses on whether or not the cognitive function of elderly adult can be improved with interventions. The data we will use data was collected from an experimental trial called "ACTIVE." [@tennstedt2013active]. The ACTIVE study began in 1996, and continued for about 10 years, patients were . The trial began with 2,082 participants, and includes measurements for subjects that passed away before the trial was completed. This study measures the outcomes of cognitive intervention in older adults, ages 65 and older. The recorded measurements include, patient characteristics, such as their age, gender, education, and baseline score. The participants were divided into 4 sub-groups, a control group, and 3 treatment groups, that measure Reasoning, Memory, and Processing Speed. The treatment groups received specialized training over 5-6 weeks, a subset within these groups had also received additional booster training.

We specifically seek to understand how a patients years of education effect their cognitive function in the Reasoning treatment group. We will use Mixed Effect models to capture this. We have included an addition term "Baseline_Reasoning" to account for the difference in scores patients began with, we will also consider the effect boosters may have on a patients reasoning outcome. In our model testing we included years, age, and gender.  





## Data

In this study we will use data collected by researches at 6 institutions; Indiana School of Medicine, John Hopkins University, Pennsylvania State University, Wayne State University, Hebrew Senior Life, and the New England Research Institute [@rebok2014ten].

These observations were recorded over a 10 year period, measurements were taken at the first phase, then at year 3, year 5, and year 10. The participants were divided into 4 outcome groups, a control group, and 3 treatment groups that were separated by Reasoning, Memory, and Processing Speed. 

The variables of interest are Age (patient age), YEARSEDUC (years of education a patient has received), Years (year the observation is recorded at), Gender(Female/Male), and an additional mutated variable, "Baseline_Reasoning". We will focus on the "Reasoning" outcome measure in our analysis.




## Methods


In this project we opted to use Mixed Effect models to capture the relationship between patient outcome and year of education. To further explore this relationship, we considered other explanatory variables such as age, gender, baseline score, and what year a patient's observation was recorded at.

We believe this model type is suitable for the data type, Mixed Effect models allow us to observe the individual slopes and intercepts for each patient. In a study assessing cognitive function, this feature is very useful, the model type provides insight on where a patient begins, and how 

All models were tested in R-Studio, using the lme4 package.

We will interpret various summary statistics, such as BIC, AIC, t-values, and correlation outputs to assess the effect combinations of explanatory variables (education, years, age) may have with the outcome (reasoning). 




```{r results = "hide"}
library(tidyverse)
library(geeM)
library(lme4)

source('cleaning_active.R')

activeLong_new <- activeLong |> 
  group_by(AID) |> 
  filter(
    INTGRP %in% c("Reasoning Training", "Control"),
    Years <= 5
    ) |> 
  mutate(
    years_more3 = if_else(Years>=3, 1, 0),
    INTGRP = relevel(INTGRP, ref="Control")
    ) |> 
  drop_na(Reasoning, Years, YRSEDUC, AgeAtBaseline, INTGRP, GENDER)
```

## Results

On average, the baseline scores of participants who received reasoning training were 2.81 points higher compared with those who did not (controlling for gender, years of education, and age at the beginning of the study). Among the intervention group before Year 3, reasoning scores increased by an additional 0.83 points with each year. This means that while scores increased for both groups within the first three years, they increased more steeply for the intervention group. After Year 3, however, reasoning scores among the intervention group decreased, on average, by an additional 1.63 points compared with the control group. This means that after Year 3, while all participants' scores decreased, the decrease was steeper among the intervention group.

When comparing our final model to a model without random slopes using an Anova test, the p-value is below 0.05, meaning we can reject the null hypothesis that the random slopes do not improve the model. 

```{r results = "hide", echo = FALSE}
rsn_mod2 <-  lmer(
  Reasoning ~ INTGRP*years_more3*Years + YRSEDUC + AgeAtBaseline + GENDER + (Years | AID), 
  data = activeLong_new, 
  REML = TRUE)

rsn_mod2_new <-  lmer(
  Reasoning ~ INTGRP*years_more3*Years + YRSEDUC + AgeAtBaseline + GENDER + (1|AID), 
  data = activeLong_new, 
  REML = TRUE)

anova(rsn_mod2_new, rsn_mod2)
```

The residuals of the final model appear relatively symmetrically distributed around $y=0$; however, the final model tends to slightly overestimate reasoning scores at the lower extreme and underestimate at the higher extreme.

```{r results = "hide", echo = FALSE}
activeLong_new %>%
  ungroup() |> 
  drop_na(Reasoning, Years, YRSEDUC, AgeAtBaseline, INTGRP, GENDER) %>%
  mutate(Pred = predict(rsn_mod2, newdata = .)) %>% 
  mutate(Resid = Reasoning - Pred) %>%  
  ggplot(aes(x = Pred, y = Resid)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = .2) + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
  theme_classic()
```

The Q-Q plot of the intercept and years shows that the distribution of our random effects is approximately normal, with some deviation toward the higher and lower extremes.

```{r}
#intercept
qqnorm(ranef(rsn_mod2)$AID[, "(Intercept)"])
qqline(ranef(rsn_mod2)$AID[, "(Intercept)"])

#years
qqnorm(ranef(rsn_mod2)$AID[, "Years"])
qqline(ranef(rsn_mod2)$AID[, "Years"])
```

## Conclusions

When taking conclusions from studies like ACTIVE, it is important to understand not only how intervention affects participants in absolute terms, but also how this relationship changes over time. Results from the model suggest that, while the training may have statistically significant improvements on reasoning in the short term, after three years, reasoning deteriorates faster, and participants return to the baseline. 

There are several limitations to our conclusions. The ACTIVE study was composed of volunteers who were not necessarily representative of the general population, especially in age and education, and participants who were older with lower cognitive function were more likely to drop out. By only looking at the first five years of the study, we hoped to lessen the impact of attrition bias, but the greater missigness in the later years might still make it more difficult to generalize our findings. 

In using a linear mixed-effects model, we assume a linear relationship between reasoning scores and years, which may not fully capture the shape of the data. LMMs also require us to drop or impute missing data, which may introduce bias if data is not missing at random. Additionally, the standard errors are only valid if the covariance model is correct.
